title_exact.en: Guidelines on the Use of Generative AI for Teaching and Learning

issuer.en: Institute for Innovative Teaching and Learning (I²TL), University of Luxembourg — contact I2TL@uni.lu

version_line.en: Version 1.0 · 16 February 2026 · 19 pages · for students AND teachers

nature.en: A foundational framework, not a disciplinary code: it explains how to use generative AI critically, ethically and transparently, and refers misconduct to the existing academic procedures. Anchored in the EU AI Act's approach: risk levels, transparency, human oversight, bias awareness.

structure.en: 1 Introduction (p.3) · 2 Guidelines for learning (p.4) · 3 AI tools supported by UL (p.5) · 4 Using GenAI effectively and responsibly (p.6) · 5 Guidelines for teaching (p.9) · 6 Assessment adaptation (p.12) · 7 Resources (p.16) · Appendix 1 disclaimers (p.18) · Appendix 2 student checklist (p.19). This session covers the student sections: 2, 3, 4 and the two appendices.

sub.en: the course rules always come first

verbatim.en: In the absence of explicit course directives, students MAY use generative AI to support their learning — within academic integrity, transparency, and respect of third-party rights.

caveats.en: the syllabus PRIMES · a course can restrict or forbid

anecdote.en: The default rule became permissive after the community consultation — the openness is deliberate, not an oversight.

detail.en: Name the tool(s) and version you used.
The purpose: brainstorm, draft, translate, debug…
The extent of the use — a paragraph, the structure, the whole draft.
Edited, corrected, rewrote, integrated — the output is a material, not a result.
How sources and claims were validated against reliable references.

example.en: « I used Copilot to brainstorm the outline; all arguments and sources are mine and verified. »

prompts_tip.en: Teachers may require your prompt history, a usage log and your verification evidence — keep your conversations.

annex_note.en: Appendix 1 provides ready-to-use disclaimers per category (brainstorming, proofreading, translation, code, content generation) — copy and adapt. Footnote of the appendix: those examples were themselves generated with Copilot, then revised.

line.en: YOU are the source — the AI polishes

detail.en: You know the answer; the AI works on the surface: proofreading, form, organising your own ideas.
You are learning the topic: summaries and syntheses of complex material help, but you check omissions, distortions and inventions against reliable sources.

line.en: You delegate what you cannot verify

detail.en: You depend on the AI for claims you cannot check — or the AI replaces the assessed learning objective itself. Hallucinations, fabricated citations, overconfidence.

frame.en: risk level ↑ = verification ↑ · never a ban

detail.en: Submitting AI output as entirely your own without disclosure; letting AI be the central intellectual contribution when the assessment targets YOUR reasoning; impersonation.
Generating or altering data, results, citations or evidence; citing unverified or non-existent sources.
Chaining tools to hide AI involvement or to circumvent integrity safeguards.
Personal or sensitive data into AI tools; other people's data or protected course material into external tools; uploading protected teaching material without authorisation.
Using AI against the course rules — in exams and controlled assessments above all.

footer.en: 10 practices = potential misconduct (§4 p.8) · unless the course explicitly allows · in doubt → BEFORE

supported.en: Copilot + UL account = THE supported choice · your data stays in UL's M365

outside.en: outside → paid with your data · personal / sensitive = NEVER

equity.en: course REQUIRES AI → a free path must exist

line.en: standard procedure · solid evidence required · a detector alone ≠ proof · your rights protected

detail.en: The existing UL academic-conduct procedure applies — these guidelines create no new tribunal.
A presumed « AI detection » is not a sufficient basis: detectors are unreliable and biased against non-native writers.
Drafts, prompts, versions: showing your process is your best defence — one more reason to keep them.

big.en: Before you submit — the final test

items.en: Course rules checked (allowed · restricted · forbidden — ask if unclear)
Disclosure ready (+ prompt log if required)

final.en: « I can explain and defend the work in my own words, including in an oral follow-up. »

big.en: The course rules say if you MAY — the law says what you MUST declare

since.en: enforced since 2 Aug 2026 · AI Office + national authorities

detail.en: Chatbots and interactive AI systems must tell you that you are dealing with AI, not a human — unless it is obvious from context. Article 50(1): a duty of the system's provider, and your right as a user.

Article 3(60), verbatim: « AI-generated or manipulated image, audio or video content that resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events and would falsely appear to a person to be authentic or truthful. » NOT every generated image: a stylised illustration or an obviously synthetic diagram is not a deepfake. What you publish that IS one must be labelled as artificially generated (article 50(4)); for evidently artistic, creative or satirical works the disclosure may be limited so it does not hamper the work.

short.en: Generated content is marked by design

detail.en: Article 50(2): providers of generative systems must mark outputs in a machine-readable format so AI-generated or altered content is detectable. The tools do it for you — your side of the duty is simple: never strip or conceal the mark, which is also the guidelines' red line on concealment. And if your tool does NOT mark? That is the tool provider's infringement, never yours — the law does not ask YOU to watermark anything. Your protection is your written disclosure and your kept prompts.

Deployer duties, article 50(4): a deepfake you disseminate must be labelled; an AI-generated or manipulated TEXT published to inform the public on matters of public interest must disclose its artificial origin — unless a human has reviewed it and someone assumes editorial responsibility. Purely personal, non-professional use is outside the Regulation (article 2(10)) — but coursework you hand in or publish is not « purely personal ».

punch.en: you BUILD a tool → you become a PROVIDER · emotion inference in education = FORBIDDEN (art. 5(1)(f))

what.en: IN FORCE — transparency (art. 50), enforcement of prohibitions (art. 5, applicable since 2 Feb 2025) and of general-purpose model duties (art. 53–55: documentation, copyright policy, training-data summaries)

short.en: IN FORCE · transparency art. 50 · prohibitions art. 5 · GPAI art. 53-55

what.en: High-risk systems (Annex III) — including EDUCATION: admission, evaluation of learning outcomes, exam proctoring (postponed by the 2026 Omnibus)

short.en: high-risk EDUCATION (annex III) — admission · grading · proctoring

what.en: High-risk AI embedded in regulated products (Annex I)

a.en: The PROVIDER makes or distributes the AI tool (OpenAI, Mistral, the startup you found…). The DEPLOYER uses it under their own name for something that reaches other people. As a student you are usually a simple user; you act as a deployer when you PUBLISH what the AI made, and you become a provider the day you BUILD a tool that others use.

q.en: My tool does not mark its images — must I add a mark?

a.en: No. The machine-readable mark (art. 50(2)) is the TOOL provider's legal duty — you have neither the obligation nor the technical means to watermark content yourself. What is yours: (1) in coursework, ALWAYS say you used AI — the one-sentence disclosure of the guidelines, whatever the tool; (2) if you publish a deepfake, label it visibly (« AI-generated ») — a plain written mention is what the law expects from you; (3) never remove an existing mark. Good practice: prefer tools that signed the Code of Practice.

q.en: Does this apply to EVERY generated image?

a.en: Three different rules, three different answers. Machine-readable marking: every generated output — but it is the tool's job, not yours. The visible « deepfake » label: ONLY content matching art. 3(60) — it resembles real people, places or events and could pass for authentic; a stylised illustration, a papercut scene or a diagram needs no legal label. The university disclosure: YES, every AI use in your coursework, whatever the content — that rule comes from the UL guidelines, not from the AI Act.

q.en: Does the label make the AI the author?

a.en: No. The mark describes the PROCESS (art. 50: « artificially generated or manipulated »), never the authorship — like « photograph » does not credit the camera. Copyright law is a separate question, and it protects YOU: under EU law a work is protected when it reflects a human's own intellectual creation through free and creative choices (CJEU Infopaq, Painer) — your conception, direction, iterations and selection make you the author of an AI-assisted work; only content generated with no human creative input has no author at all (European Parliament resolution of 10 March 2026). The honest and legally accurate form is the DOUBLE mention: your name as author, « made with generative AI » as process — which is also this deck's own practice.

channels.en: Complaint Tool (art. 85, open to any natural or legal person) · downstream-provider channel (art. 89(2), for breaches of art. 53–55) · Whistleblower Tool. Over 180 organisations signed the Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-generated Content.
